content: There is a statistically significant positive correlation between human IQ and height within national populations. However, this correlation is weak, as variations in height account for only about 4% of the variation in IQ. This does not imply that short individuals cannot be highly intelligent, nor does it suggest that changes in physical height directly influence cognitive ability. Intelligence is influenced by a multitude of factors, and individuals with a wide range of intelligence levels can be observed at any given height. Similar correlations between height and intelligence have been observed during early and late childhood as well as adulthood, across both developed and developing countries. These correlations persist even after controlling for variables such as social class and parental education. The reasons behind the association between height and intelligence remain unclear. One possible explanation is that height may serve as an indicator of nutritional status, prenatal maternal stress, or overall mental and physical health during development. However, studies have shown that common genetic factors contribute to variations in both height and intelligence, accounting for part of the observed correlation. Additionally, both height and intelligence may be influenced by adverse early environmental exposures. A large twin study investigating the relationship between height and intelligence found that shared environmental factors (59%) and shared genetic factors (35%) significantly contribute to the observed correlation. Another hypothesis suggests that the correlation may be linked to the relationship between height and self-esteem. The theory posits that height during teenage years boosts self-esteem, which in turn enhances academic performance and cognitive outcomes. Interestingly, it is not an individual's adult height that matters most, but rather their height during high school. For example, tall men who were short during high school tend to earn incomes similar to short men, while short men who were tall during high school earn incomes comparable to tall men. This finding appears to rule out discrimination as a factor, as it would be difficult for employers to know their employees' past heights. Instead, it suggests that another underlying factor is influencing this relationship.
